questions.knowledge_point: Visualizing Intersections of Uncountable Families of Indexed Sets
questions.problem: Let $I=[0,1]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}=[0,i]\times [0,1].$ Which of the following represents ${⋂}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the intersection of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *all* the sets:

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for all}\,\,k\in I}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}=[0,0.5]\times [0,1]={(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,0.5],b\in [0,1]}.
$$

This represents a rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(0.5,0),$ $(0.5,1),$ and $(0,1)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082768/assets/5b882f3fb0e7b44eb2df3a510260574e5c4a4d85842a9c0d65515f1a40894756.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}=[0,i]\times [0,1]={(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,i],b\in [0,1]}
$$

is the rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(i,0),$ $(i,1),$ and $(0,1).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082768/assets/cb530698591dbd71a8058d9faa0c60b636dc654f21e92d65ec8295aeaa67355a.png)

The intersection of all these rectangles is the line segment ${0}\times [0,1]:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082768/assets/704f8f6f0666d09bb2b8a25eab0548c3eb808e2c9d394d2ae873de35cb0112d1.png)

questions.problem: Let $I=[0,1]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}=[-1,1]\times [-i,i].$ Which of the following represents ${⋂}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the intersection of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *all* the sets:

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for all}\,\,k\in I}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}=[-1,1]\times [-0.5,0.5]={(a,b)\,:\,a\in [-1,1],b\in [-0.5,0.5]}.
$$

This represents a rectangle whose vertices are at $(1,-0.5),$ $(1,0.5),$ $(-1,0.5),$ and $(-1,-0.5)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082768/assets/f0a530434b8ac38fdb4cb517f22e121892c8b7c635c702c1cd9fccb2961aee18.png)

$$
{X}_{i}=[-1,1]\times [-i,i]={(a,b)\,:\,a\in [-1,1],b\in [-i,i]}

is the rectangle whose vertices are at $(1,-i),$ $(1,i),$ $(-1,i),$ and $(-1,-i).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082768/assets/6982658bd8ce0e3c81953309ed9f2a70d1e56bbfce8af8862a32da66bf19e638.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082768/assets/34a3addbdcf3d5348805f494ed2e427f21f6ad424b0d9d2a411dae9f99b2fb7a.png)

questions.knowledge_point: Sketching Cartesian Products of Special Sets in the Coordinate Plane
questions.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S=R\times N$ in the Cartesian plane?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B={(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=R\times N
$$

 
contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is a real number and whose $y$-coordinate is a natural number.

$$
S={(x,y)\,:\,x\in R,\,y\in N}
$$

To visualize $S,$ consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $1.$

$$
{S}_{1}={(x,1)\,:\,x\in R}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082768/assets/f8808e4c35775c754dab0bf328a8d129e423009e18ec5f4b962461eba2afcea2.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $2.$

$$
{S}_{2}={(x,2)\,:\,x\in R}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{2}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082768/assets/a51fe9dc5bf7c55b01f72a45d4b88bde4653f0d3da85c1231b0d54c76a6e8c81.png)

We can create the subsets ${S}_{3},{S}_{4},{S}_{5},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}R\times N & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup … \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in N}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $R\times N$ as the set of horizontal lines shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082768/assets/7ae3c488e60d3dcda304649e575a7d2efc54be7262a54d0455550af420c39b68.png)

questions.knowledge_point: Sketching Cartesian Products of Special Sets in the Coordinate Plane
questions.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S={Z}^{-}\times {Z}^{-}$ in the Cartesian plane?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B={(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S={Z}^{-}\times {Z}^{-}
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is a negative integer and whose $y$-coordinate is a negative integer.

$$
S={(x,y)\,:\,x\in {Z}^{-},\,y\in {Z}^{-}}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{-1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $-1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is negative integer.

$$
{S}_{-1}={(-1,y)\,:\,y\in {Z}^{-}}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{-1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082768/assets/37ad5627c3fb7cc89e751bb697e01ac7fecaf2712e230b6e3812ad9137d5cd46.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{-2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $-2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any negative integer.

$$
{S}_{-2}={(-2,y)\,:\,y\in {Z}^{-}}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{-2}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082768/assets/97ebcac85477b8e88564ab67d59c926d5faa72138c8a31d80d3b89895f33668c.png)

We can create the subsets $…{S}_{-5},{S}_{-4},{S}_{-3}$ similarly. Our Cartesian product $S$ is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =…{S}_{-5}\cup {S}_{-4}\cup {S}_{-3}\cup {S}_{-2}\cup {S}_{-1} \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in {Z}^{-}}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize ${Z}^{-}\times {Z}^{-}$ as the set of points in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082768/assets/a756e53554cb9184d96a52b83038fbd6b00b21d0a12cc658aebb5010e917fd03.png)

questions.knowledge_point: Visualizing Unions of Uncountable Families of Indexed Sets
questions.problem: Let $I=[0,1]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}=[-i,i]\times {1-i}.$ Which of the following represents ${⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the union of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *at least one* set:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for at least one}\,\,k\in I}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}=[-0.5,0.5]\times {0.5}={(k,0.5)\,:\,k\in [-0.5,0.5]}.
$$

This represents a horizontal line segment from the point $(-0.5,0.5)$ to the point $(0.5,0.5)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082768/assets/509d3e8d3bce0b422cad7e7f02377468cacc0de3a4e45647c12fef15f2c9991f.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}=[-i,i]\times {1-i}={(k,1-i)\,:\,k\in [-i,i]}
$$

is the horizontal line segment from the point $(-i,1-i)$ to the point $(i,1-i).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082768/assets/21859c2ac02ba80d47672bf2fab25f7358feb921bc5b546c1e8c783c2819bea3.png)

As $i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following triangle that represents the union ${⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082768/assets/5b5715ba2a1b71a9f5aef52882ed62ba2fe1610c143224914430f79fdc8f06b5.png)
